reading.body:
One federal digital forensics opening, paying $128,740 to $178,390, is the entire listing count for this function across ten job sources.

The role sits at the U.S. Postal Service in Richmond, California, and it is a security position rather than an AI research or infrastructure one. Digital forensics work is downstream of systems that already exist: someone has to examine what a deployed system did. That places it closer to the operational end of AI than to the compute, buildings, and power that make AI possible, and nothing in this data connects it to data center capacity or electricity demand.

The count of one is the important number. Ten sources are queried, including federal openings, aggregated listings, remote boards, European listings, and company career boards, and together they surface a single posting. That is either a genuinely thin market for this function or a limit of what these sources capture, and the data cannot distinguish between the two.

What this does not cover: no history, so there is no way to tell whether one is high, low, or typical. No employer beyond a single federal agency, so no read on private-sector demand. No seniority distribution, no remote share, and no comparison to other security functions. A single posting supports no conclusion about AI hiring, and it should not be read as one.
